subject: Archaeology
title: Roman Roads: Paths That Lasted 2,000 Years
description: A micro-lesson that makes Roman Roads: Paths That Lasted 2,000 Years usable.

hook.text: Roman roads were so well built that some are still in use today, 2,000 years after construction.

buildup.text: The road network spanned 250,000 miles — enough to circle Earth ten times. It connected every corner of the empire.

discovery.text: Roads were built in layers: rubble base, gravel fill, and fitted paving stones, all crowned for drainage.

twist.text: Many modern European highways follow the exact routes of Roman roads. The empire's planners chose the best paths first.

climax.text: Scholars mapped every known Roman road digitally. The network looks like a modern transit map with Rome at the hub.

punchline.text: All roads led to Rome. Many of them still do.

quiz.question: How large was the Roman road network at its peak?
options: About 50,000 miles connecting major cities only
Around 250,000 miles — enough to circle Earth ten times
Over 1 million miles including unpaved paths

details.summary: Rome built over 80,000 kilometers of paved roads across its empire, engineered with layered foundations of gravel, sand, and stone that made them remarkably durable. Many Roman roads survive today, and some modern European highways still follow their straight routes across the landscape.
details.whyItMatters: Roman roads were the internet of the ancient world — they moved armies, goods, laws, and ideas across vast distances. Their engineering excellence set a standard unmatched for over a thousand years after Rome's fall.
takeaways: Rome built over 80,000 km of paved roads across the empire
Layered foundations of gravel, sand, and stone ensured durability
Many modern European routes still follow Roman road alignments

faq.question: How were Roman roads constructed?
faq.answer: Workers excavated a trench, then built up layers: large stones at the base, smaller gravel and sand for drainage, and paving stones on top with a slight crown for water runoff. Ditches on each side channeled rainwater. The total depth could exceed one meter.

faq.question: Why were Roman roads so straight?
faq.answer: Roman engineers used a surveying instrument called a groma to establish straight sightlines between points. Straight roads were faster for military marches and reduced construction complexity. Where hills or rivers required detours, curves were kept as gentle as possible.
